name: Slate-Olive
lede: Slate-Olive is a grayish green first dated by Ridgway in 1912, the darkest and least saturated of the library's three slate colors.

sections.title: The least saturated of the three
sections.body: Ridgway's 1912 standard places this hue on plate XLVII, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS system classes it as a dark greenish gray, block 156 [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary is cited by the same 1955 circular, without a separate date of its own [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[serpent]], [[saul]], [[deep-greyish-blue-green]] and [[nickel-green]], at 5.4, 5.5, 4, 5.5, 5.7 and 6.1 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to Slate-Olive in 610 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.6 percent, as photographed [2]. It plays a midtone more than half the time, 55 percent, with highlight and shadow uses roughly split the rest of the way [2]. Henri Rousseau, Francesco Guardi and Berthe Morisot all use it well above the archive's average rate, and its strongest single match is a 1588 handscroll, Song Xu's *Eighteen Views of Huzhou*, where it covers 72 percent of the canvas [2].

The earliest dated match is a 1275 Japanese Buddhist painting, *Monju with Five Hair Knots*, more than six centuries before Ridgway's plate, which only shows a similar screen color was photographed there, not that the name or a matching pigment existed that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
